objective: Build a self-introduction with an f-string
prompt: Define two variables: `name` holding your name and `role` holding what you want to learn. Then print one Chinese sentence that says who you are and what you want to learn, built from those two variables with an f-string. The starter shows the sentence template to use.
starter:
name = ""
role = ""
# Print the Chinese line with one f-string, using both variables.
# Template: 我是{name}，我想学{role}   ("I am {name}, I want to learn {role}")

checks.code: assert isinstance(name, str) and name.strip(), 'name must be a non-empty string'
assert isinstance(role, str) and role.strip(), 'role must be a non-empty string'

llm_rubric.criteria: Did the learner really use two variables instead of hard-coding the string?

reference:
name = "Mian"
role = "Agent development"
# \u-escapes keep this answer CJK-free while still printing the Chinese line.
print(f"\u6211\u662f{name}\uff0c\u6211\u60f3\u5b66{role}")
explanation: An f-string embeds values with {} and avoids manual concatenation. Assign name and role before printing, otherwise the sentence has holes in it. The printed line stays Chinese on purpose, so the check matches it literally; the escape sequences above are just that same sentence written in ASCII. The automated checks can only see that both variables hold non-empty strings and that the printed line has the right shape — whether you really used an f-string instead of a literal is something your own code has to show.

objective: Compute the bytes needed to load a model into VRAM
prompt: A model has 7 billion parameters loaded at fp16 precision (2 bytes per parameter). Compute the total weight size and store it in `weight_bytes`.
starter:
params_billion = 7
bytes_per_param = 2
# compute and assign weight_bytes

llm_rubric.criteria: Does the learner understand that the parameter count is in billions?

explanation: 7 billion = 7 x 10^9. Times 2 bytes each gives 1.4 x 10^10 bytes, about 13 GB. That is weights only; a real deployment also needs KV cache and activations.

objective: Spot which code actually prints a model response
prompt:
Which of these produce visible output? (multi-select)

A. `print(model.generate(prompt))`
B. `model.generate(prompt)` on its own line
C. `print(model(prompt))`
D. `answer = model.generate(prompt)` followed by `print(answer)`
reference: A, C and D. B is valid Python but Jupyter echoes the last expression; a plain script prints nothing.
explanation: You have to capture the result and print it. B looks fine in Jupyter because the last cell expression is echoed, but in a .py script or a server call nothing is shown -- the most common "the model ran but nothing happened" cause.
